summary: Extends the PASSporT token from RFC 8225 so it can carry a signed assertion of authorization for values in the SIP Resource-Priority header field. That header is used to prioritize communications resources, and the signature lets others trust the claim.

plainLanguage.summary: In an emergency, some calls get to skip the line. This adds a tamper-proof signed pass showing that a call really is allowed to skip.

questions: what is the passport rph claim
how does a verifier handle an rph passport
what is ppt rph in stir
subtitle: A signed PASSporT claim that proves a caller is allowed to use SIP Resource-Priority values.

tldr.problem: The SIP Resource-Priority header asks the network to give a call priority when resources are scarce, but it could be spoofed and abused by unauthorized parties.
tldr.mechanism: A new PASSporT extension, ppt value "rph", carries an "rph" claim whose "auth" array lists the signed r-values, so a verifier can check that the caller is authorized for them.
tldr.outcome: Receivers, even in other network domains, can trust a signed Resource-Priority assertion, and a failed check means the call is treated as an ordinary call.

today: RFC 8443 is a Proposed Standard from August 2018 and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends RFC 8225.

sections.title: Why Sign the Resource-Priority Header
sections.content:
PASSporT (RFC 8225) is a token format based on JSON Web Token. Together with STIR (RFC 8224), it lets an authority on the calling side give cryptographic assurance about the calling party's telephone number.

RFC 4412 defines the SIP Resource-Priority header field, which lets user agents, PSTN gateways and proxies influence the priority a session gets when network resources are scarce. The problem is that this header could be spoofed and abused by unauthorized entities, which could lead to misuse of network resources during congestion.

This RFC extends PASSporT so that an authority can sign the header and assert the caller's authorization. How the extension is used for real-time communications is outside its scope, and it is meant for environments where the signer can be verified as authoritative.
sections.plainLanguage: A priority lane only works if nobody can sneak into it. This gives the people who guard the lane a way to check a signed ticket.

sections.title: The rph Claim and the ppt Value
sections.content:
The creator of the PASSporT adds a ppt value of rph to the token header. The claims MUST contain an rph claim, and any verifier must understand the ppt extension to process the token.

The rph claim asserts authorization (auth) for the r-values in the Resource-Priority header, where an r-value is a namespace, a dot and a priority. The claim's value is an object with one or more keys, each holding a JSON array of strings that match the r-values in the header. The example in the RFC uses ets.0 and wps.0.

The signature is made as in RFC 8225 using the full form of PASSporT; the compact form is not specified here. The certificate used must have authority over the namespace of the claim, and there is only one authority per claim. If intermediaries add or drop r-values, they must generate a new rph claim and sign it with their own authority.
sections.plainLanguage: The token has a label saying it is a priority pass, and inside it a list of the exact priority levels the caller may use, stamped by someone who is allowed to hand them out.

sections.title: Authentication Service Behavior
sections.content:
A SIP authentication service builds the rph claim following the steps in Section 4.1 of RFC 8224. It derives the value from the Resource-Priority header, based on policy for service-specific use of r-values.

It does so by verifying the calling user's privilege for the header based on the user's identity. The RFC says that authorization might be derived from customer-profile data or access to external services.

RFC 4412 allows several namespace and priority pairs in one header or across several headers. An authority is responsible for signing all the content of a Resource-Priority header for which it has the authority. The result travels in the SIP Identity header with ppt="rph".
sections.plainLanguage: Before handing out the pass, the guard checks who you are and whether you are on the list.

sections.title: Verification Service Behavior
sections.content:
The verification service MUST extract the value under the auth key in a full-form PASSporT with a ppt of rph. It must also verify the iat value, as RFC 8224 requires.

If the signature validates, the verifier can treat the claim as proof that the caller is authorized for the listed Resource-Priority values. Priority treatment then follows local policy for that communication service.

If validation fails, the verifier should infer that the caller is not authorized. The Resource-Priority header SHOULD be stripped from the SIP request and the network entities should treat the call as an ordinary call. What a user agent does on receiving an INVITE with an rph claim is largely implementation policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The person at the gate checks that the pass is real. If it is, you get to skip the line. If not, you wait like everyone else.

sections.title: Room for More Information
sections.content:
Other facts about the caller could matter for authorization, such as the device subscription, institutions the caller is associated with, or categories of institutions. The STIR and PASSporT frameworks could secure all of these.

The rph claim may therefore carry extra information fields. A new IANA registry holds possible values of the rph array, but the details of how the claim carries other data are left to future specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: The pass could later say more about you, like which team you belong to. This RFC only leaves a space for that.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added the claim rph (Resource Priority Header Authorization) to the "JSON Web Token Claims" registry, with the IESG as change controller and Section 3 of this RFC as the specification.

IANA also created an entry for type rph in the "Personal Assertion Token (PASSporT) Extensions" registry and a new "PASSporT Resource Priority Header (rph) Types" registry. Each entry holds the type name and the specification describing it. It starts with the single value auth, and new types need Specification Required.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of names got two new entries so nobody else reuses them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 8224, Section 12, apply. The rph extension MUST only be sent with a SIP INVITE when the Resource-Priority header conveys the communication's priority. To avoid replay and cut-and-paste attacks, the recommendations in Section 12.1 of RFC 8224 MUST be followed.

Using the extension requires knowing the authentication, authorization and reputation of the signer, including validating the signature and the certificate chain to a trust anchor. A signer may only sign Resource-Priority content it is authorized for, and before signing it MUST have a secure method to authenticate the end user or device. Verification MUST include checking that the signer is authoritative for the namespace in the PASSporT.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the real guard may stamp passes, the guard must know who is asking, and an old pass cannot be copied and used again.
